 Screen Love in Disguise, our K-drama pick of the week, blends Boys’ Love parody with corporate thrills
 By Ankita Chandra 
 Published: 16 Nov 2026, 8:00AM | 4 min read .
 Advertisement GENRE : Romance, dual identities 
 WHERE TO WATCH : Prime video 
 YOU WILL LOVE IT IF YOU LOVE:  
 Under cover missions 
 Queer romance parodies 
 Strong female protagonists 
 Elite family secrets 
 Slapstick humour 
 t2 RATING : 3/5
 For those acquainted with the Boys’ Love genre, an entertainment category that has risen rapidly in popularity among young fans, it is natural to wonder why K-dramas have largely brushed past queer representation. While occasional releases such as Semantic Error do convey the industry’s awareness of the massive impact of queer romance on the Asian entertainment scene, Korean shows remain heavily dependent on heteronormative conventions of love. Prime Video’s ongoing K-romance, Love in Disguise , capitalises on both sides of the coin: the lingering awkwardness around queerness in the Korean entertainment scene and the parallel surge in demand for love stories beyond the heteronormative spectrum. The plot follows a complex romance between the privileged heir to an elite business family, who is accused of murder, and his bodyguard, who is actually a female cop working undercover as a man. 
 Advertisement Though the styling department has not paid much attention to making the central plot device of the disguise work, Seol In-ah, who plays the undercover cop Kang Jae-hee, makes up for it with a committed performance, aptly adopting the gait and body language of a man. In the introductory scenes, Jae-hee is seen throwing punches and kicks at a group of scammers, just after being asked for her Instagram username by a high-school girl who is simply smitten by her good looks, obviously under the impression that Jae-hee is a man! 
 For a show that falls short in its styling efforts, the dialogues must repeatedly reinforce the image the story needs to create for its protagonist. From the waitress at the restaurant where Jae-hee and her colleagues are regulars, to the high-school girl who is smitten by Jae-hee’s looks at a convenience store, and even her colleagues, everyone keeps harping on the fact that she is often mistaken for a man. But Jae-hee is more than just a woman who acts like a man. After her impressive fight with the scammers, the fierce cop who wreaked havoc at the crime scene suddenly reveals her vulnerable and chirpy feminine side. Jae-hee has a crush on one of her colleagues and blushes at his concern for her, much like the highschool girl had blushed at the sight of Jae-hee. She also faces some unique challenges at work, as she is never allowed to use the women’s restroom because she so strongly resembles a man. 
 At this point, the vision behind Jae-hee’s character becomes clear. The character sketch aims to show how identity can never be compartmentalised through static perceptions, and how gender is very much a social construct that needs a more fluid definition. But, once again, weak styling undermines much of the impact of what the plot attempts to convey. Simply having a cropped hairstyle and wearing sporty T-shirts and hoodies does not really make a woman look like a man. More effort was needed to make the actor look the part. 
 If there is a woman disguised as a man, there must be a man who falls for her despite the disguise, creating the intended queer tension the series aims for. It is a faint glimmer of hope for Boys’ Love fans, but a glimmer all the same, considering the utter lack of variation in the stereotypical man-woman relationships that K-dramas have largely portrayed over the years. Enter Yoon Yi-jun (Yim Si-wan), a privileged and somewhat obsessive heir and soon-to-be successor to an elite business empire. He takes care to pose with his wrist turned towards the camera to promote his company’s unreleased timepiece as a guerrilla marketing tactic while shaking hands with the president. He can also spot even the slightest variation in the angle at which a painting in his living room is tilted. Quite an attractive go-getter, one might think, until he is accused of murdering his subordinate, and his meticulous eye for detail begins to be perceived as a major symptom of psychopathic tendencies! 
 A criminal investigation follows, and if you have not guessed it already, the task falls to Jae-hee’s department. Her colleagues decide to place her as an undercover police officer in Yi-jun’s house, posing as his bodyguard, and the Boys’ Love parody kicks off immediately. Through banter, slapstick scenes and plenty of romantic tension, the two begin falling for each other, although Jae-hee’s cover must remain intact until she succeeds in her mission. New episodes of Love in Disguise drop every Monday and Tuesday on Prime Video.
 Characters we treasure... 
 YIM SI-WAN AS  YOON YI-JUN : An actor who can move from the cosy warmth of Summer Strike to the chilling suspense of Strangers from Hell is certainly capable of handling the comparatively flatter role of a rich, bratty businessman. But what makes his performance stand out, and makes it clear that he is perfectly suited to the role, is the eccentric humour he brings to the character. In the initial episodes, it is difficult to be entirely certain that Yi-jun is not the murderer, thanks to the subtle touches added by the actor, such as a creepy grin and blank, sly stares. Si-wan’s soft and delicate features also add to the overall queer tension of the narrative, something that may not have been possible with an actor with a roughand-tough masculine profile.
 Advertisement SEOL IN-AH AS KANG JAE-HEE:  With the Business Proposal star’s graceful handling of her manly female character, Yim Si-wan is simply not the only heartthrob on the show! Kicks and punches aside, Jae-hee’s character also strikes a rare balance between outward physical strength and emotional vicissitudes, presenting a fuller, more rounded picture of both masculinity and femininity.
